title: Burst Penumbra: latency vs cost snapshot
executive_summary: This memo explores the "penumbra" effect: a latency tail-shadow around brief concurrency bursts where amortization of warm state reduces cost but increases p99. We compare three mitigation strategies (always-prewarm, lazy-on-demand, hybrid micro-preheat) across representative session mixes and report tradeoffs in cost-per-1k-tokens and p99 latency under a microburst profile.
key_findings: 1) Prewarming (steady minimal hot slots) reduces p99 by ~18–35ms for short bursts but increases baseline $/1k tokens by ~6–9%. 2) Lazy-on-demand is cheapest per-token at steady state but suffers large p99 spikes during super-short bursts (2–10x higher p99). 3) Hybrid micro-preheat (fast ephemeral preheat on predicted surge) can capture ~70% of latency benefit of full prewarm while keeping cost within +2–3% of lazy. 4) KV-cache hit patterns strongly modulate the break-even point: high hit-rate sessions favor lazy strategies more than stateful multi-turn chat workloads.
measurement-environment: Instances: g4dn-equivalent GPU cluster with mixed instance widths. Model: 7B decoder-only baseline (fp16) and 7B quantized int8 variant. Workload: synthetic sessionized traffic with Poisson baseline and injected microbursts (30s windows) at 10x concurrency. Metrics: p50/p90/p95/p99 latencies (ms), tokens generated, $ estimate per 1k tokens (asset-backed cost model), warm-slot fraction.

sensitivity_notes: - KV-cache hit-rate sweep: when hit-rate >= 0.6, lazy margin improves and break-even shifts toward LAZ for $/1k tokens. - Cold-start time composition: kernel cold penalty (~18ms) + model load (~90ms) dominates the first-token tail; reducing model load via small resident layers materially shifts tradeoffs. - Prediction accuracy for hybrid preheat: >70% correct preheat within 5s of burst start recovers 60–80% of prewarm p99 benefit.
recommendation: 1) For latency-sensitive SLA tiers (p99 < 200ms), adopt a hybrid micro-preheat policy with a small always-hot floor (warm-slot-fraction ~0.2) plus predictive micro-preheats. 2) For cost-sensitive public tiers, retain lazy defaults but expose burst-mitigation toggles in Console (toggle: aggressive-preheat / conservative). 3) Instrument KV-hit telemetry and session-type labeling to allow model-level policy decisions (e.g., stateful chat -> prefer hybrid). 4) Next-step: run A/B on real traffic for two weeks, track p99 tail events and delta $/1k; iterate preheat thresholds.

full_content:
Background:
The 'penumbra' metaphor: short bursts create a shadow of elevated tail latency that persists even when average utilization is low. This memo quantifies that shadow across three operational strategies and sketches tradeoffs.

Methodology:
- Traffic: baseline Poisson 50rps with sessions sampled from two cohorts: Q (short-turn single-query FAQ flows) and Chat (multi-turn stateful). Injected microbursts: 30s windows at t=300s,600s etc with multiplicative factors 2x,5x,10x.
- Runtime knobs: resident slots (0 - 0.8 fraction), prefetch size, KV-cache TTL.
- Cost model: blended GPU-hour+network+storage amortized per token; normalized to $/1k tokens for easy comparison.

Highlights (expanded):
- Prewarm keeps model in-resident more often: effective load balancing reduces queuing and kernel startup overhead. Result: p99 tail compressed but at a steady cost uplift.
- Lazy-on-demand benefits from ideal steady-state efficiency: if bursts are rare and KV-hits high, it's cheapest. But tail is exposed: cold penalties stack and cause long p99 spikes.
- Hybrid micro-preheat: brief ephemeral preheats triggered by surge detectors (simple rate threshold on ingress) or prediction models. Works well if we can preheat <5s before burst; suffers if predictions are late/false-positive.

Benchmark caveats:
- These runs used synthetic bursts; customer traffic shapes differ. The hybrid break-even depends on prediction quality and the relative cost of false preheat.
- Cost model excludes long-tail operational overhead (on-call, extended troubleshooting) which favors lower tail strategies.
